column1: What is the Carnot efficiency formula, and what theoretical ceiling does it impose on a motorcycle engine with peak combustion temps ~2500K and exhaust temps ~1100K?
column2: η_Carnot = 1 - (T_cold/T_hot), both in Kelvin. With these values, the theoretical ceiling is approximately 56%.

column1: Why does real-world brake thermal efficiency of high-performance motorcycle engines (38-42%) fall far short of the Carnot limit?
column2: Due to irreversibilities: incomplete combustion, heat transfer losses through cylinder walls, pumping losses during gas exchange, and mechanical friction in the rotating assembly.

column1: How many crankshaft degrees does one complete four-stroke Otto cycle require, and what are the four strokes?
column2: 720 degrees (two full revolutions): intake, compression, power, exhaust.

column1: What is the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio (AFR) for gasoline, and what does lambda (λ) represent?
column2: Stoichiometric AFR ≈ 14.7:1 by mass. Lambda is the ratio of actual AFR to stoichiometric ideal; λ=1.0 means exactly stoichiometric.

column1: What lambda value and AFR range is typical for wide-open-throttle maximum power in a naturally aspirated four-stroke race engine, and why richer than stoichiometric?
column2: λ ≈ 0.88 (approx 12.9:1 AFR), within the broader 12.5:1-13.2:1 range. Richer mixtures cool combustion via fuel evaporation latent heat, protecting piston crown/exhaust valve from thermal stress and ensuring all oxygen finds a fuel partner.

column1: Why is running lean (λ > 1.0, e.g., λ=1.05) dangerous under load on a race bike despite fuel economy benefits?
column2: Lean mixtures raise peak cylinder temperatures dramatically, collapsing the thermal margin to detonation and risking catastrophic engine failure.

column1: Why does a motorcycle transmission need multiple discrete gear ratios instead of a single fixed ratio?
column2: Because the engine produces peak torque only in a narrow RPM band (e.g., 8,000-12,000 rpm), while rear wheel speed must span from ~200 rpm (walking pace) to ~2,800 rpm (top speed)—a two-order-of-magnitude range requiring mechanical advantage changes to keep the engine in its optimal torque window.

column1: For a first gear pairing of a 14-tooth drive gear and 38-tooth driven gear, what is the gear ratio and what happens to torque vs. output shaft speed?
column2: Ratio = 38:14 ≈ 2.71:1. Output shaft speed is 0.37 rev per engine rev, but torque is multiplied by 2.71x (minus gear mesh friction losses).

column1: What are the three stages of torque multiplication in a motorcycle drivetrain from crankshaft to rear wheel, and their typical ratio ranges?
column2: 1) Primary drive reduction (crankshaft to clutch basket): 1.8:1 to 2.1:1. 2) Gearbox ratio (varies by gear). 3) Final drive sprocket ratio: 2.5:1 to 3.2:1. Combined, overall drive ratios span ~12:1 (first gear) to ~4.5:1 (top gear).

column1: What are the three primary channels through which a four-stroke motorcycle engine dissipates waste heat, and their approximate share of total fuel energy?
column2: Exhaust system (~30%), cooling system (~25%), radiation plus oil cooling (remaining balance). Useful work at the crankshaft is only ~35-40%.

column1: What are the key trade-offs between air-cooled and liquid-cooled motorcycle engine designs?
column2: Air-cooled: simpler, lighter, no water pump losses, but poor heat flux capability, uneven thermal gradients (hot exhaust valve seat vs cooler intake side), and poor transient response (heat soak in stop-and-go traffic). Liquid-cooled: two-stage heat transfer path via closed-loop coolant gives dramatically improved uniformity and heat flux capacity at the cost of added weight/complexity.

column1: In MoTeC i2 Pro telemetry analysis, what are the three primary sensor domains used to diagnose motorcycle powertrain behavior?
column2: 1) Engine performance instrumentation (crank speed, throttle position, manifold pressure). 2) Drivetrain mechanical feedback (clutch line pressure, gearbox output shaft speed, chain tension load cells). 3) Chassis dynamic response (rear wheel speed, triaxial accelerometer data, suspension travel potentiometers).
